title: Hundred Days
wiki_lead:
The Hundred Days, commonly referred to as The War of The Seventh Coalition or Napoleon’s Hundred days (French: les Cent-Jours IPA: [le sɑ̃ ʒuʁ]) marked the period between Napoleon's return from ten months of exile on the island of Elba to Paris on 20 March 1815 and the second restoration of King Louis XVIII on 8 July 1815 (a period of 110 days). This period saw the War of the Seventh Coalition (French: Guerre de la Septième Coalition), a commonly-used name for the Hundred Days, which includes the Waterloo campaign and the Neapolitan War (Naples and Austria) as well as several other minor campaigns. The phrase les Cent Jours (the Hundred Days) was first used by the prefect of Paris, Gaspard, count of Chabrol, in his speech welcoming the king back to Paris on 8 July.
Napoleon returned while the Congress of Vienna was sitting. On 13 March, seven days before Napoleon reached Paris, the powers at the Congress of Vienna declared him an outlaw, and on 25 March, Austria, Prussia, Russia, and the United Kingdom, the four Great Powers and key members of the Seventh Coalition, bound themselves to put 150,000 men each into the field to end his rule. This set the stage for the last conflict of the Napoleonic Wars, the defeat of Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo, the second restoration of the French kingdom, and the permanent exile of Napoleon to the distant island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821.

Background


Napoleon's rise and fall
The French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars pitted France against various coalitions of other European nations nearly continuously from 1792 onward. The overthrow and subsequent public execution of Louis XVI in France had greatly disturbed other European leaders, who vowed to crush the French Republic. Rather than leading to France's defeat, the wars allowed the revolutionary regime to expand beyond its borders and create client republics. The success of the French forces made a hero out of their best commander, Napoleon Bonaparte. In 1799, Napoleon staged a successful coup d'état and became First Consul of the new French Consulate. Five years later, he crowned himself Emperor Napoleon I.
The rise of Napoleon troubled the other European powers as much as the earlier revolutionary regime had. Despite the formation of new coalitions against him, Napoleon's forces continued to conquer much of Europe. The tide of war began to turn after a disastrous French invasion of Russia in 1812 that resulted in the loss of much of Napoleon's army. The following year, during the War of the Sixth Coalition, Coalition forces defeated the French in the Battle of Leipzig.
Following its victory at Leipzig, the Coalition vowed to press on to Paris and depose Napoleon. In the last week of February 1814, Prussian Field Marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher advanced on Paris. grok_lead: The Hundred Days ( Cent-Jours) refers to the period of Napoleon Bonaparte's return to power in France from 20 March 1815, when he entered Paris after escaping exile on Elba, until 8 July 1815, when the Bourbon Restoration was reinstated under Louis XVIII. This interval, spanning approximately 110 days despite the name, marked Napoleon's brief second reign as Emperor of the French, during which he navigated internal political challenges and external threats from a resurgent coalition of European powers. Upon his arrival, Napoleon faced initial resistance from royalist forces but advanced to Paris without major combat, prompting King Louis XVIII's flight and the dissolution of loyal troops. He reorganized the government, appointing loyal ministers and convening the French Chambers, while promising constitutional reforms to broaden support, including the Acte additionnel of 1815, which introduced elements of representative government and expanded suffrage. However, these efforts were overshadowed by the rapid formation of the Seventh Coalition, comprising Britain, Prussia, Austria, Russia, and allies, which declared him an outlaw and mobilized against France. Napoleon's military campaign culminated in the Battle of Waterloo on 18 June 1815, where his forces were decisively defeated by Anglo-Prussian armies under the Duke of Wellington and Gebhard Leberecht von BlÃ¼cher, due to tactical errors, delayed reinforcements, and superior coalition coordination. This loss precipitated his abdication on 22 June, the surrender of Paris on 31 July, and his exile to Saint Helena, ending the Napoleonic Wars and reshaping European alliances through the Congress of Vienna's framework. The episode highlighted Napoleon's enduring charisma and military acumen amid logistical constraints and diplomatic isolation, but ultimately underscored the unsustainable nature of his imperial ambitions against unified opposition.
